clue.text: Chap familiar with Pugin's Rolls, green leather seats, shiny alloyed wheels

definitions.text: Chap familiar with Pugin's Rolls, green leather seats

indicators.note: to wheel is to turn round, so the letters of the two words are spun into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A car buff admires a Rolls-Royce with green leather seats and gleaming alloy wheels.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rolls looks like a car; here it is the parliamentary rolls of the Palace of Westminster, whose interiors Augustus Pugin designed, and green leather benches fill the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lindsay Hoyle is Speaker of the House of Commons, so he knows its Pugin interiors and green benches intimately.

clue.text: India's openers put on healthy runs, which gets up one's nose

parts.note: the first two letters of India
hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: India's opening batsmen score briskly, which irritates the opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets up one's nose' is the British idiom for annoying someone, but read literally it describes medicine travelling up the nostrils.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhaler is a device that delivers medicine breathed in through the mouth or nose.

clue.text: No. 1 detectives upset having to accept rubbish, overbearing command

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the junk goes inside the overturned pieces
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so these pieces read from bottom to top

parts.note: NO is the usual abbreviation for number
the numeral one looks like the letter I
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's detective branch
tat is cheap, worthless stuff

explanation.surface: Top detectives are annoyed at being forced to swallow nonsense from a domineering boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No.' is the standard abbreviation for number, and 'upset' in a down clue means turned upside down, so the whole No. 1 detectives group reads bottom to top before the rubbish goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Dictation is the act of giving orders authoritatively, imposing terms without discussion.

clue.text: You folks in the Southern US putting down Yankee friend

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a letter down moves it to the bottom of the word

parts.words: You folks in the Southern US
parts.note: y'all is the Southern American contraction of 'you all'
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Southerners being rude about a friend from the North.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting down' sounds like insulting the Yankee, but it sends the Y of Y'ALL to the foot of the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is a partner or supporter, someone on your side.

clue.text: 1 should know these domestic, local laws

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Lindsay Hoyle (1 across) is Speaker of the House, and 'according to Hoyle' means following the rules
second meaning: rules particular to one household or venue

explanation.walkthrough: Edmond Hoyle wrote the standard rulebooks for card games, so the Speaker of the House surnamed Hoyle doubly should know the House's rules.
explanation.definitionFit: House rules are customs or regulations that apply only in a particular home, club or game table.

clue.text: Oik starts to yomp over Brecon Beacons, ending in Llandeilo

indicators.note: the starts of the next four words supply their first letters
the end of the Welsh town's name supplies its final letter

explanation.surface: A lout marches across the Brecon Beacons in Wales, finishing at the town of Llandeilo.
explanation.walkthrough: To yomp is military slang for a laden march; the Brecon Beacons are Welsh mountains used for army training.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for a rough, uncouth young man, a lout.

clue.text: Making a mistake bedding American stud?

indicators.note: to bed something is to embed it, so the letter is taken inside the word

parts.note: erring means going wrong

explanation.surface: Someone errs by sleeping with a handsome American man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stud' suggests a virile man in the bedroom; here it is a small piece of jewellery, and the question mark marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is one kind of earring, a single post worn through the lobe.

clue.text: Sack my thick, craven, unwanted Speaker

indicators.note: to sack a town is to ransack it, throwing everything into disorder

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a dim, cowardly Speaker one wants rid of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' reads as dismiss, fitting the surface, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Kevin McCarthy was the US House Speaker voted out of office by his own party in 2023.

clue.text: Liberal Tory pact inane; absolutely no way

indicators.note: liberal can mean free or loose, so the letters are interpreted freely

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A Liberal scorns a silly coalition deal with the Tories as out of the question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks like a party in British politics; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means under no circumstances, refusing a deal whatever the cost offered.

clue.text: Having principles here once in Rome (and elsewhere round about)

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the Latin pair of words sits around the other piece

parts.note: et al is the Latin abbreviation for 'and others' or 'and elsewhere'
hic is Latin for 'here', the language once spoken in Rome

explanation.surface: Moral standards held here in ancient Rome, and in other places nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are Latin, as the clue's 'once in Rome' hints: the scholarly abbreviation for 'and others' wraps around the Latin word for 'here'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethical person acts according to moral rules, which is what having principles means.

clue.text: Eco warrior finally laid to rest in lavish EU tomb

indicators.note: the warrior's last letter is buried inside the rearranged letters as in a grave
something lavish is extravagantly done up, so the letters are elaborately rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of warrior

explanation.surface: An environmental activist is buried in an extravagant European Union mausoleum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eco warrior' is a red herring phrase; 'Eco' alone is the definition, the Italian novelist. The rearranged EUTOMB becomes UMBETO, with R laid inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Umberto Eco was the Italian novelist and semiotician who wrote The Name of the Rose.

clue.text: Feeling unwell, perhaps? Not half!

parts.note: ill means sick
say means for example, perhaps, as in 'a big city, say'

explanation.surface: Asked whether they are under the weather, someone replies emphatically yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', not a request to halve something.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic British exclamations of agreement, meaning certainly or you bet.

clue.text: Ordinary boring menials ground bits of wheat

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into, so the letter goes inside the rearranged menials
ground means milled or crushed, so the letters are broken down and re-formed

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Dull servants mill grain in a flour mill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like dull; it means drilling into, putting O into the anagram SEMLINA (from 'ground').
explanation.definitionFit: Semolina is coarse granules of durum wheat used for pasta and puddings.

clue.text: Torches New Forest site

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An arsonist burns a spot in the New Forest, a national park in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Forest' reads as the English park, but 'New' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To torch something is to deliberately ignite it, which is exactly the phrasal verb.

clue.text: A top sociologist, I abandoned gin cocktail for water when in Paris

indicators.note: the letter I is left out, abandoned by the word

parts.note: a martini is a cocktail of gin and vermouth
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: A leading sociologist quit gin cocktails and switched to water while living in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Harriet Martineau (1802-1876) is often called the first woman sociologist.
explanation.definitionFit: Harriet Martineau was a pioneering Victorian social theorist, regarded as a founder of the discipline.

clue.text: Mum is collecting good, soft rock

indicators.note: collecting means gathering in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: mama is a word for mother

explanation.surface: Mother picks up some gentle pop music records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soft rock' suggests easy-listening music; here it is molten rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Magma is the molten material beneath the Earth's crust, rock in a fluid state.

clue.text: Power consuming Baker "un-British"? Correct

indicators.note: consuming means eating, so one piece is swallowed inside the other

parts.note: might means strength or power

indicators.note: the B, standard abbreviation for British, is removed from the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A political figure named Baker is accused of being unpatriotic, and the charge is upheld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'un-British' strips the B from BAKER, leaving AKER, which MIGHT then consumes.
explanation.definitionFit: To make right is to put a wrong to rights, rectifying or setting straight.

clue.text: Clampdown regularly culled fowl

indicators.note: every other letter is removed at a steady interval, leaving alternate ones

explanation.surface: A crackdown routinely slaughters poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the first, third, fifth and so on letters of Clampdown.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel fattened for the table, a kind of domestic bird.

clue.text: Clergyman, one sat in church seat for the early show?

indicators.note: the clergyman and the numeral are seated inside the church bench

parts.note: a pew is a bench in a church
Rev, short for Reverend, is a clergyman's title
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A vicar sitting alone in a pew for an early service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early show' could be a dawn church service; here it is a showing before release.
explanation.definitionFit: A preview is a showing of a film or play to an audience before its official opening.

clue.text: 1 Republican leaving a sleazy, empty bar

indicators.note: the letter for Republican departs from the word

parts.note: 1 across, Lindsay Hoyle, is the Speaker

indicators.note: emptied of its inside, the word keeps only its outer letters

explanation.surface: The Speaker, with no Republican present, finds a seedy deserted bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 1 is the answer to 1 across, Lindsay Hoyle, so it gives SPEAKER; R leaves to give SPEAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A speakeasy was an illicit drinking den during US Prohibition.

clue.text: Word for the opposite 4 of Caesar, J

parts.note: 4 down is ALLY, and the great ally of Julius Caesar was Mark Antony
Caesar, J is written surname first with an initial, as in an index; Caesar's ally written the same way ends with the initial of his first name, Mark

explanation.surface: Seeking the word for the friend of Julius Caesar, listed in an index.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caesar, J' puts the surname first with an initial, as in a register; Mark Antony written the same way is ANTONY, M, so the J signals the M.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a term meaning the reverse of another, as hot is to cold.

clue.text: Filmed Butler, short of time, discovered jester's OTT speech

indicators.note: the word is left lacking the letter for time

parts.note: Rhett Butler is the hero of the film Gone with the Wind

indicators.note: dis-covered means its covering is taken off, so the outer letters are stripped

parts.note: Yorick is the dead jester whose skull Hamlet holds

explanation.surface: A film character finds a jester's overblown monologue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short of time' drops a T from RHETT; 'discovered' strips Y and K from YORICK, the jester in Hamlet, leaving ORIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhetoric often means bombastic language, inflated speech designed to impress more than inform.

clue.text: Book set in Waterloo Rd, Erith

indicators.note: the answer is set inside the address, spanning the words

parts.note: Erith is a town in south-east London; the letters run across the words

explanation.surface: A novel set on a street in Erith, south-east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a noun for a novel; it is the verb, as in reserving a table.
explanation.definitionFit: To order a meal or ticket is to book it, reserving it in advance.

clue.text: 21 specialist artist discontented with gold frames

indicators.note: frames means surrounds, with a piece of gold on each side of the artist's remains

parts.note: OR is gold in heraldry; frames, plural, puts it on both sides

indicators.note: with its contents removed, the word keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An unhappy painter whose work sits in gilt frames.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 21 is RHETORIC, so a 21 specialist is a master of rhetoric; OR stands on each side of AT.
explanation.definitionFit: An orator is a skilled public speaker, an expert in persuasive speech.

clue.text: Sebastian embracing King Charlie

indicators.note: embracing means hugging, holding the letter inside

parts.note: Sebastian Coe is the British Olympic runner and athletics administrator
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Seb Coe hugs King Charles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like King Charles; it is slang for cocaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie is slang for cocaine, which is also called coke.

clue.text: Rug tint one introduced to rugged European?

indicators.note: the numeral is brought into the other pieces

parts.note: hardy means tough, robust
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A colour for a carpet, offered to a tough continental man?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug' looks like a carpet; it is slang for hair, especially a toupee.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair dye colours hair; rug is slang for a wig or head of hair.

clue.text: MSc in Agronomy backs eating this type of veg!

indicators.note: backs says the hidden letters are read backwards
the phrase is eating the answer, holding its letters inside across the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A master's graduate in crop science endorses eating chemical-free vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left the hidden word without an indicator and put 'eating' in the definition; 'eating' is the signal that the letters are held inside the phrase, so the definition is just 'this type of veg'.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic produce is grown without synthetic fertilisers or pesticides.

clue.text: Duff up tiny bloke, initially earn more cash if you do this!

definitions.text: more cash if you do this!

parts.note: to duff up and to work over both mean to beat someone up
Tiny Tim is the small boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of earn

explanation.surface: Beat up a small man and you'll make more money, the clue claims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duff up' is British slang for beating someone up. Tiny Tim is the Cratchits' son in A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: Working beyond normal hours usually earns extra pay, so this is how you get the extra money.
